title: Algebraic Characterization of k-Fold Origami Constructibility
description: Formalizes the conjectured algebraic characterization of k-fold origami constructibility: k simultaneous folds can construct exactly the p_{k+1}-smooth degrees (all prime factors ≤ the (k+1)-th prime). Proves strict hierarchy (each fold level adds one prime), monotonicity, and algebraic completeness (every degree is eventually constructible).

originalContributions: IsSmooth p n: formal p-smooth number predicate with closure properties (one_smooth, prime_smooth, smooth_mul)
IsKFoldConstructible d k: k-fold origami constructibility via p_{k+1}-smooth degrees
Strict hierarchy witnesses: 5 separates 1-fold from 2-fold, 7 separates 2-fold from 3-fold, 11 separates 3-fold from 4-fold
constructible_mono: more folds implies more constructible degrees
eventually_constructible: every d > 0 is k-fold constructible for some k (algebraic completeness)
Composite degree classification: 6, 9, 10, 30, 42 at each fold level
meta.assumptions: None. 0 axioms, 0 sorries. All results follow from the IsKFoldConstructible definition. The definition itself encodes the conjectured pattern for k ≥ 3 (which is mathematically open).

overview.historicalContext: Alperin and Lang (2006) established the algebraic characterization of origami constructibility for 1-fold (3-smooth degrees) and 2-fold (5-smooth degrees) operations. The natural conjecture is that k-fold origami corresponds to p_{k+1}-smooth degrees, where each additional fold unlocks the next prime. This formalization explores the consequences of this conjecture, proving internal consistency via strict hierarchy witnesses, monotonicity, and algebraic completeness.
overview.problemStatement: What is the precise algebraic characterization of k-fold origami constructibility for k ≥ 3? The conjectured answer: k simultaneous folds can construct exactly the degrees whose prime factors are all ≤ the (k+1)-th prime.
overview.text: Formalizes p-smooth numbers and k-fold origami constructibility. Proves the strict hierarchy: each fold level adds exactly one new prime as a constructible degree. Every degree is eventually constructible with enough folds.
overview.proofStrategy: Define IsSmooth and IsKFoldConstructible using Mathlib's Nat.nth for prime enumeration. Use concrete prime bounds (from Nat.Prime.Nth) for small k. Prove strict hierarchy by showing the (k+2)-th prime is (k+1)-fold constructible but not k-fold. Prove algebraic completeness using add_two_le_nth_prime.
keyInsights: The smooth number framework cleanly captures k-fold constructibility: p-smooth = all prime factors ≤ p
Each fold level adds exactly one new prime to the constructible set
Monotonicity follows from nth_strictMono on the infinite set of primes
Algebraic completeness uses p_n ≥ n+2: take k = d to ensure all prime factors of d are below the prime bound
The conjecture for k ≥ 3 is mathematically open — this file explores consequences, not proves the conjecture
prerequisites: Prime numbers and the infinitude of primes
Smooth numbers: integers whose prime factors are bounded
Prime counting functions and Nat.nth from Mathlib

sections.title: Smooth Numbers
sections.summary: Defines IsSmooth p n (n > 0 and all prime factors ≤ p). Proves one_smooth, prime_smooth, smooth_mul, and not_smooth_of_large_prime.
sections.mathContext: A positive integer $n$ is **$p$-smooth** if every prime factor of $n$ is $\leq p$. Equivalently, $n$ can be written as a product of primes from $\{2, 3, \ldots, p\}$. The 3-smooth numbers are $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, \ldots\}$ (powers of 2 and 3).

sections.title: k-Fold Origami Constructibility
sections.summary: Defines foldPrimeBound k = Nat.nth Prime k (the (k+1)-th prime) and IsKFoldConstructible d k = (k ≥ 1 ∧ IsSmooth (foldPrimeBound k) d).
sections.mathContext: The prime bound for fold level $k$ is $p_{k+1}$: $k=1 \to 3$, $k=2 \to 5$, $k=3 \to 7$, $k=4 \to 11$. Degree $d$ is $k$-fold constructible iff $d$ is $p_{k+1}$-smooth.

sections.title: Degree Classification at Each Fold Level
sections.summary: Proves concrete classifications: degree 3 is 1-fold, degree 5 is NOT 1-fold but IS 2-fold, degree 7 is NOT 2-fold but IS 3-fold, degree 11 is NOT 3-fold but IS 4-fold.
sections.mathContext: The separating primes: $5$ separates 1-fold from 2-fold ($5 > 3$ but $5 \leq 5$), $7$ separates 2-fold from 3-fold ($7 > 5$ but $7 \leq 7$), $11$ separates 3-fold from 4-fold ($11 > 7$ but $11 \leq 11$).

sections.title: Strict Hierarchy and Monotonicity
sections.summary: Proves strict hierarchy witnesses at each level. Proves constructible_mono: k-fold ⊆ (k+1)-fold via nth_strictMono.
sections.mathContext: The constructibility hierarchy: $\text{1-fold} \subsetneq \text{2-fold} \subsetneq \text{3-fold} \subsetneq \cdots$. Each inclusion is strict, witnessed by the next prime. Monotonicity follows from $p_{k+1} < p_{k+2}$.

sections.title: Composite Degree Classification
sections.mathContext: $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ is 3-smooth, $9 = 3^2$ is 3-smooth, $10 = 2 \cdot 5$ is 5-smooth but not 3-smooth, $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ is 5-smooth, $42 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$ is 7-smooth but not 5-smooth.

sections.title: Algebraic Completeness
sections.summary: Proves every d > 0 is k-fold constructible for some k. Uses add_two_le_nth_prime: p_{d+1} ≥ d+2 > d ≥ all prime factors of d.
sections.mathContext: Since $p_n \geq n + 2$ and all prime factors of $d$ are $\leq d$, taking $k = d$ gives $p_{k+1} \geq d + 2 > d$ as the prime bound, ensuring all prime factors are below it.

conclusion.summary: Formalizes the conjectured algebraic characterization of k-fold origami: p_{k+1}-smooth degrees. The definition encodes the conjecture; the theorems verify its internal consistency (strict hierarchy, monotonicity, completeness). For k=1,2 this recovers Alperin-Lang 2006; for k≥3 the conjecture is mathematically open.
conclusion.implications: The smooth number characterization suggests a deep connection between origami fold complexity and prime factorization. The hierarchy compass ⊊ 1-fold ⊊ 2-fold ⊊ 3-fold ⊊ ... mirrors the prime sieve: each level adds one prime to the constructible set.
openQuestions: Can multi-fold origami solve ALL polynomial equations (is it algebraically complete)?
What is the minimum number of simultaneous folds needed to solve an equation of degree n?
